model: Lower Columbia River fall Chinook spawning IP (Busch et al. 2011)
validation_result: 89% of ODFW/WDFW-mapped spawning reaches scored high or very high IP against 43% of the whole network (chi-squared 394.84, d.f. 4, p < 0.001); population IP did not predict current abundance (p = 0.47); reach IP vs EDT adjusted R2 = 0.46. The network's tidal lower limit was set at, and checked against, the lowest documented spawning on the same state maps (PDF pp. 2-3), so the 89 % comparison is not wholly independent.
quote: We estimated the channel width of each reach using a regression developed by Steel and Sheer (2003); this regression uses basin drainage area (km2) and mean annual precipitation (mm) as predictors of channel width
validation_quote: The IP model scored 89% of the ODFW/WFDW-demarked spawning reaches as high or very high potential habitat for spawners
note: Channel width (bankfull) modelled for every reach with the Steel and Sheer (2003) regression on drainage area and mean annual precipitation; large mainstem widths set by hand from the DEM and other hydrologic sources (PDF p. 3). The regression's training widths are not described. No discharge variable and no surrogate. Confinement is valley width / bankfull width from 10-m DEMs (PDF p. 4). Access also limited by tidal influence (<= 3.5 m above sea level), the 350 m elevation contour and waterfalls (>= 3-4.6 m), none of which has a variable here; the < 4 m access width is at seasonal low flow. Early-view PDF, pages are PDF pages.

quote: Reach-average bankfull channel dimensions were predicted using empirical hydraulic geometry equations relating drainage area (in m2) to bankfull width (w) and bankfull depth (h)
note: Bankfull width and depth from hydraulic-geometry regressions on drainage area fitted to field data (Wood-Smith and Buffington 1996, n = 23; Zynda 2005, n = 83; Fig. 3, p. 607) on a 20-m DEM NetMap network. Mean annual flood (Q2) from a USGS regional regression is used for scour, not for the habitat criteria. Unconfined = floodplain wider than twice bankfull width (p. 608). Criteria are Paustian (2010)'s, not Burnett's. Not validated: predictions are 'first-order approximations that require field validation' (p. 618). Egg scour (>50 % probability of scour to 30 cm) is an incubation criterion with no matching variable here.

model: NOAA SWFSC historical IP for coho, Chinook and steelhead, south of Cape Blanco
quote: We attempted to evaluate this assumption by estimating regional models for mean annual discharge as a function of catchment area and mean annual precipitation. To accomplish this, we assembled discharge data for stream gages with at least 20 years of data
note: Juvenile coho. Mean annual discharge modelled per DEM reach (Miller 2003 network from a 10 m DEM and PRISM precipitation) from a regression of gauges (>=20 yr, unimpaired) on catchment area and mean annual precipitation (n = 29, r2 = 0.988; a separate San Francisco Bay model), PDF pp. 11-13. Valley constraint = DEM valley-floor width / active channel width, where active channel width is computed from discharge (PDF p. 12); no threshold is converted to width. Not validated against fish: the gradient-barrier check on the Mad River was impressionistic, and the coho temperature mask was set from historical presence (calibration). Bjorkstedt et al. (2005) apply it unchanged in the NCCC domain.

General agreement is reported, with false positives named for sockeye (Chulitna drainage; Chikuminuk and Upnuk lakes) and Chinook (Chulitna drainage), and no statistic. The authors call the models hypotheses for future validation (p. 80). Not fully independent: the AWC, aerial counts and telemetry were among the 'known patterns of salmon abundance' used to develop the models (p. 80), and the floodplain metrics were checked against AWC presence before use (p. 24).
quote: Channel width measurements from studies throughout the Nushagak and Kvichak watersheds recorded in the AFFI (ADFG 2013) were used to develop power relationships between width and mean annual flow
validation_quote: This corresponds with what little is known about chum salmon spawning areas
note: 'Channel size' in the spawning tables read as modelled channel width: w = 1.710 Q^0.471 from AFFI field widths regressed on modelled MAF, which is the Parks & Madison (1985) regression on flow accumulation and precipitation (pp. 35-36). Bankfull or wetted is not stated. The access rule (>12 % gradient) uses gradient only.

model: Thompson EDU juvenile rearing capacity (CART on FDIS CPUE)
quote: We used the empirical method developed by Davies et al. (2007) to calculate bankfull width of each macroreach based on drainage area and precipitation
note: Bankfull width modelled with the Davies et al. (2007) equation Wb = 0.042 A^0.48 P^0.74, fitted to orthophoto widths in Puget Sound (input listed as field_measurement); checked against 155 FDIS sites, R2 = 0.73 (p. 22). The CART splits were fit on field-measured FDIS bankfull width and gradient. Confinement was tested and dropped (p. 66). Distribution is a separate occurrence model plus barrier passage probabilities by obstacle height (Table 2.3), with no gradient barrier. Not validated: the 10-fold cross-validation (p. 66) is the CART pruning step, part of fitting, and it rejected every split; the classes used were grown with a relaxed complexity parameter. The authors list field validation of capacity as further work (p. 83).

model: NCCC TRT fall-run Chinook spawning IP
quote: estimating regional models for mean annual discharge as a function of catchment area and mean annual precipitation
note: Fall-run Chinook spawning only: Agrawal's IP machinery (Burnett et al. 2003; Agrawal et al. 2005) with Chinook-specific suitability curves (p. 89), two discharge curves, the conservative one reducing IP above 50 m3/s. Coho and steelhead in this report use Agrawal's curves unchanged (agrawal2005). The report says the conservative curve better matches known spawning distributions but does not test it; recorded as no validation. Regional discharge regressions fitted to gauges (Agrawal et al. 2005).
